text: In one day, two point eight trillion dollars vanished from America's biggest companies. If you stacked it in hundred-dollar bills, the pile would pass the tallest building in America before it even reached a billion dollars. Then it would keep climbing, past the planes and through the edge of space, until it stood more than three thousand kilometers high, seven times higher than the space station.
So who ended up with all of that money? Surprisingly, nobody did, and by the end of this video you'll see exactly why.

Here's what actually happened that Thursday, November 5th. The S&P 500, which follows five hundred of America's largest public companies, fell four point four percent, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell about five and a half percent. Analysts pointed to a mix of reasons, but on the business side it came down to chips. Two big chip companies, Qualcomm and Arm, put out results and forecasts that disappointed investors, and that reopened a question hanging over the whole market: will the huge sums being poured into AI data centers actually pay off?

To find where the money went, let's peek inside the company at the center of that question, Nvidia, the chip maker whose processors run much of today's AI. On Wednesday, one Nvidia share cost about two hundred dollars, and by Thursday's close it was down to about a hundred and eighty-two, a drop of just over nine percent and its biggest one-day fall since April of last year. Because Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies on Earth, that nine percent came to nearly four hundred and fifty billion dollars, which in hundred-dollar bills is a stack almost five hundred kilometers tall, higher than the space station, from a single company.

But here's the strange part: Nvidia itself didn't lose a single dollar of cash that day, and to see why, you need to know how a company's value is worked out. It's one multiplication, the latest price of a single share times every share that exists. Nvidia has about twenty-four billion shares, so when one share drops by about eighteen and a half dollars, the whole company drops by eighteen and a half dollars times twenty-four billion, all at once.

And this is the part most headlines leave out. On that Thursday, about three hundred million Nvidia shares changed hands, which sounds like a lot until you compare it with the twenty-four billion that exist, because it's only about one share in every eighty. The other seventy-nine never moved, yet every one of them was re-priced at the new, lower price, because the latest price a buyer and a seller agree on becomes the price of every share.

So what happened to the actual cash? Every share that was sold that day was bought by someone else, and the buyer paid the seller in real money, so the cash didn't vanish at all, it just moved from one account to another.

That's the answer to our question. The two point eight trillion dollars was never a pile of cash sitting somewhere, it was the price tag on the whole market, and on November 5th, that price tag shrank.

That doesn't mean the drop didn't matter. Retirement accounts and pension funds own these same companies, so millions of people saw their savings shrink on paper, and a loss on paper only turns into a loss in cash when someone sells for less than they paid. Prices move the other way too, and the very next day, Nvidia was already up almost three percent.

So the next time a headline says billions vanished in a day, you'll know they weren't stolen or burned, they were just re-priced. Did you check your portfolio on November 5th? Tell me in the comments.
